COLDWAR_SOV_the_collective_leadership: January 1970. Six years after the fall of Khrushchev, the Soviet Union is governed by a troika: Leonid Brezhnev as General Secretary, Alexei Kosygin at the head of the Council of Ministers and Nikolai Podgorny as head of state. Behind the facade of unity, the Politburo balances reformers against the orthodox, Moscow against the republics and the planners against the generals. Whoever holds this balance holds the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_lenin_centenary: On 22 April 1970 the Soviet Union marks one hundred years since the birth of Vladimir Ilyich Lenin. Jubilee medals, mass rallies, new monuments and an endless stream of 'Leniniana' on television and in print turn the anniversary into the greatest propaganda campaign of the decade. The Party presents itself as the rightful heir of the revolution, and every citizen is reminded to whom the future is owed.
COLDWAR_SOV_kremlin_politics: Power in the Soviet Union does not flow from elections but from the quiet arithmetic of the Politburo. Every appointment, every retirement and every new regional first secretary shifts the balance between reformers and the orthodox guardians of the system. To rule from the Kremlin, the General Secretary must learn to count votes, reward loyalty and isolate rivals before they can do the same to him.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_24th_party_congress: From 30 March to 9 April 1971 almost five thousand delegates gather in the Kremlin Palace of Congresses for the XXIV Congress of the CPSU. Brezhnev unveils a Peace Programme for relations with the West and the guidelines of the Ninth Five-Year Plan, promising both security and a better life for Soviet citizens. The congress sets the course of the collective leadership for the years to come.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_doctrine_of_developed_so: Communism has not yet arrived, but the Party now declares that the Soviet Union has entered the stage of 'developed socialism', a long historical era in which the system perfects itself step by step. The doctrine replaces Khrushchev's bold promise of communism by 1980 with a reassuring message of stability and gradual progress. It gives ideologists such as Mikhail Suslov a firm framework and tells every citizen that the foundations are sound.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_gerontocracy_question: The men who rose under Stalin still sit at the summit of the Party. By the middle of the decade the average age of the Politburo exceeds sixty-five, and many regional secretaries have held their posts for twenty years or more. Stability of cadres has bought the leadership loyalty and calm, but it also blocks the path of younger, more capable officials. The Party must decide whether to renew its ranks or honour its veterans.
COLDWAR_SOV_renew_the_cadres: The generation of 1964 cannot govern forever. By sending veteran ministers and obkom secretaries into honourable retirement and promoting younger engineers, economists and administrators, the leadership can breathe new energy into the state. The old guard will not leave quietly, and the shake-up will cause friction throughout the Party apparatus, but a renewed cadre corps may be exactly what the Union needs to face the decades ahead.
COLDWAR_SOV_respect_for_seniority: The Party rewards those who have served it longest. Ministers, marshals and first secretaries keep their posts until they die in office, and the nomenklatura enjoys a security unknown since the revolution. The result is calm and predictable government, but also an era that later generations will call the zastoi, the Stagnation, as growth slows, corruption spreads and new ideas wait in vain for a hearing.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_1977_constitution: Long in preparation, a new Fundamental Law is to replace the Stalin Constitution of 1936. Its sixth article enshrines the Communist Party as the leading and guiding force of Soviet society, while the text proclaims the Soviet people a new historical community of many nations. The Brezhnev Constitution codifies developed socialism, broadens the formal rights of citizens and binds the republics ever more closely to the centre in Moscow.
COLDWAR_SOV_whither_the_union: Where is the Soviet Union heading? Behind closed doors, Party theorists, scientists, economists and patriots offer competing answers: a reaffirmation of the Party's leading role, a cautious opening towards the West, a socialist path independent of both blocs, or a revival rooted in Russian tradition. The leadership must decide which current of thought it will allow to shape the next generation of Soviet politics.
COLDWAR_SOV_dir_the_leading_role: The answer to every question is the Party. Ideological commissions, the Komsomol and the primary Party organisations in every factory and collective farm are ordered to strengthen discipline and political education. Deviations are to be corrected, doubts dispelled and the masses mobilised behind the line of the Central Committee. The Union will march forward as Lenin intended, guided by the vanguard of the working class.
COLDWAR_SOV_dir_convergence: Since 1968 the physicist Andrei Sakharov has circulated his essay 'Reflections on Progress, Peaceful Coexistence and Intellectual Freedom', arguing that capitalism and socialism must converge to save mankind. Instead of silencing the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, the leadership now permits an official debate on his ideas. Scientists and intellectuals sense a new thaw, while the guardians of orthodoxy see the first crack in the dam.
COLDWAR_SOV_dir_third_way: Neither the rigid orthodoxy of the apparatus nor the consumer capitalism of the West offers a convincing future. Inspired by Yugoslav self-management, the Prague reformers and the anti-colonial movements of the Third World, a circle of Soviet theorists proposes a socialism of its own: decentralised, pragmatic and open to the non-aligned world. The debate is risky, but it promises fresh answers to old problems.
COLDWAR_SOV_dir_the_russian_idea: Writers of the village prose movement, the journal Molodaya Gvardiya and patriotic circles within the Party call for a return to Russian roots: the land, the old churches and the memory of the Great Patriotic War. Elevating the Russian people as the backbone of the Union can rally soldiers and patriots behind the state. For Ukrainians, Balts and Central Asians, however, a Russian revival sounds dangerously like Russification.
COLDWAR_SOV_gosplan_directives: Gosplan, the State Planning Committee under Nikolai Baibakov, sets the targets for every factory, mine and collective farm from the Baltic to the Pacific. Millions of products, prices and deliveries must be balanced on paper before a single tonne of steel is poured. Strengthening the authority of the planners and the discipline of the five-year plans is the first step towards mastering the economy.
COLDWAR_SOV_complete_the_eighth_plan: The Eighth Five-Year Plan, covering 1966 to 1970, is the most successful of the post-war era. Industrial output and real incomes grow at a pace no later plan will match, helped by Kosygin's reforms and the opening of Siberian resources. Now its final year must be completed with honour: unfinished factories commissioned, targets reported as fulfilled and the foundations laid for the next plan.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_kosygin_reform_question: Since 1965 Premier Alexei Kosygin's reform has judged enterprises by sales and profit rather than gross output, rewarded workers with bonuses and granted managers more autonomy. Since the Prague Spring of 1968, however, the Politburo views any loosening of central control with suspicion, and the ministries are quietly rolling the reform back. Should the Kosygin reform be deepened, or allowed to fade away?
COLDWAR_SOV_deepen_the_kosygin_reform: Kosygin and his economists argue that the reform has failed not because it went too far but because it never went far enough. Enterprises should keep a larger share of their profits, draw up more of their own plans and answer to their customers rather than to the ministries. The branch ministries and much of the nomenklatura resist, but the Premier is determined to give Soviet industry the incentives it lacks.
COLDWAR_SOV_enterprise_self_financing: Under full khozraschyot, or economic accounting, Soviet enterprises must cover their costs from their own revenues instead of relying on endless subsidies from the state budget. Profitable factories may reinvest and reward their workers, while loss-making ones face pressure to modernise or merge. For managers it means freedom; for the trade unions it raises the spectre of lost jobs and harder work.
COLDWAR_SOV_lessons_from_budapest: Since 1968 Janos Kadar's Hungary has quietly experimented with its New Economic Mechanism, combining central planning with market prices, enterprise autonomy and a modest private sector. Hungarian shops are full while Soviet shelves stand empty. Instead of viewing Budapest with suspicion, Moscow could send its economists to study what works and adapt the lessons to Soviet conditions, and win the gratitude of a loyal ally in the process.
COLDWAR_SOV_legalise_the_cooperatives: Behind the facade of the planned economy lies a vast second economy of private tailors, mechanics, builders and traders, tolerated because everyone depends on it. Legalising small cooperatives would bring these activities into the open, generate tax revenue and fill the gaps the state cannot. For the nomenklatura, who profit from the shadows, it means the end of lucrative privileges, and they will not forgive it.
COLDWAR_SOV_cybernetic_planning: In 1962 the cybernetician Viktor Glushkov proposes OGAS, a nationwide automated system linking every enterprise to regional computing centres and to Gosplan in Moscow. In 1970 the Politburo shelves the plan, wary of its cost and of the transparency it would bring. What if the leadership decides otherwise and entrusts the planned economy to computers and mathematics instead of paperwork and guesswork?
COLDWAR_SOV_the_ogas_network: The first regional computing centres are online, and data from the factories begins to reach Moscow in hours instead of months. Now the network must be extended across the Union, connecting thousands of enterprises, ministries and planning offices into a single information system. If Glushkov's vision succeeds, the Soviet Union will possess the most advanced planning apparatus in the world.
COLDWAR_SOV_kantorovich_optimal_prices: Leonid Kantorovich, the father of linear programming, has argued for decades that optimal prices can be calculated mathematically to allocate scarce resources efficiently. His work will earn him the Nobel Prize in Economics, yet at home his ideas remain suspect as a disguised theory of the market. Adopting objectively determined valuations could bring rationality to the arbitrary prices of the planned economy.
COLDWAR_SOV_computing_centres_of_the_rep: From Kiev and Minsk to Tallinn, Tbilisi and Tashkent, each union republic receives its own computing centre and institute of cybernetics. Local engineers and mathematicians train on Soviet machines, process regional statistics and write software for their industries. The project spreads modern skills beyond Moscow and Leningrad and gives the republics a stake in the scientific future of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_ministries_restored: Khrushchev's regional economic councils, the sovnarkhozy, have been abolished and the centralised branch ministries restored. Each ministry once again commands its own empire of factories, research institutes and supply networks from Moscow. The ministers regain their power and the apparatus its order, but every ministry guards its own interests, and coordination between the branches suffers.
COLDWAR_SOV_new_union_ministries: As the economy grows more complex, new all-union ministries are created for instrument-making, mineral fertilisers, the gas industry and other specialised branches. Each brings expertise, investment and a direct line to the Council of Ministers. Each also brings new departments, new officials and new paperwork, adding further layers to an already formidable bureaucracy.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_tolkachi: No plan can foresee every missing bolt or delayed cable. Every Soviet enterprise therefore relies on its tolkachi, the 'pushers' who travel the country with favours, bribes and bottles of cognac to obtain the materials the official supply system fails to deliver. They are illegal in spirit yet indispensable in practice, keeping the factories running at the price of an ever-growing culture of informal deals.
COLDWAR_SOV_plan_fulfilment_campaigns: Red banners, honour boards and socialist competition between brigades: the Party mobilises the workforce to fulfil and overfulfil the plan. Shock workers are celebrated in Pravda, model collectives receive medals and the best enterprises are entered in the books of labour glory. The campaigns raise output and morale, even if the reported figures sometimes owe more to creativity than to production.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_ninth_five_year_plan: The Ninth Five-Year Plan, covering 1971 to 1975, is adopted by the XXIV Party Congress. For the first time the planners promise that consumer goods will grow faster than heavy industry, while the armed forces press for their own share of investment. The leadership must decide where the priorities of the coming five years truly lie.
COLDWAR_SOV_group_b_goods_for_the_people: Soviet planners divide industry into Group A, the means of production, and Group B, the consumer goods. The Ninth Plan promises for the first time that Group B will grow faster, bringing more clothing, furniture, shoes and household goods to Soviet families. Turning this promise into reality demands investment and attention that the defence industry would rather keep for itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_brezhnevka: The five-storey Khrushchyovka is giving way to a new generation of prefabricated housing. Panel blocks of nine to sixteen storeys, with lifts, larger kitchens and separate bathrooms, rise in vast new districts on the edges of every Soviet city. Millions of families leave their communal apartments for flats of their own, and the housing programme becomes one of the most visible achievements of the era.
COLDWAR_SOV_refrigerators_and_television: A refrigerator in the kitchen and a television in the living room: for Soviet families of the 1970s these are the symbols of a modern life. Factories in Minsk, Moscow and Lvov expand their output of household appliances, and the first colour sets begin to replace black and white. Every new appliance proves that socialism can deliver comfort as well as steel.
COLDWAR_SOV_group_a_means_of_production: The classic Soviet doctrine is clear: heavy industry first, for without machines, steel and energy there can be no consumer goods tomorrow. The planners direct investment towards new plants, power stations and metallurgical combines, accepting that the shop shelves will remain sparse for now. It is the proven path of the first five-year plans, and many in Gosplan see no reason to abandon it.
COLDWAR_SOV_steel_cities: Magnitogorsk in the Urals, built around a mountain of iron ore during the first five-year plans, remains the symbol of Soviet metallurgy, while the Cherepovets works near the Rybinsk Reservoir is among the most modern steel plants in the country. Expanding both secures the steel on which every other branch of industry depends, from the shipyards of Leningrad to the tractor plants of the Volga.
COLDWAR_SOV_machine_building_first: Machine-building is the heart of every industrial economy, yet Soviet factories still work with ageing lathes and outdated equipment. Prioritising machine tools, precision engineering and automation would raise productivity across all sectors and reduce dependence on imports from the West. Engineers and designers receive new resources, and the factories of Leningrad, Kharkov and Sverdlovsk lead the way.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_defence_sector_first: With the strategic balance against the United States at stake, the Military-Industrial Commission demands absolute priority for the defence sector. New arms plants, design bureaux and test ranges receive the best engineers and the scarcest materials. The marshals and the defence industry welcome the decision, while Soviet consumers once again learn to wait.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_nine_ministries: The Soviet defence industry is organised into nine ministries, from Medium Machine-Building, which builds the nuclear arsenal, to aviation, shipbuilding, radio and electronics. Each runs its own closed cities, schools, hospitals and research institutes, forming a state within the state. Coordinating them more tightly under the Military-Industrial Commission promises to make the Soviet arsenal cheaper and more efficient to produce.
COLDWAR_SOV_dual_use_factories: Tank plants that build refrigerators, missile factories that turn out vacuum cleaners and aircraft works that produce washing machines: the defence industry is ordered to dedicate part of its capacity to civilian goods. The quality is often poor and the designs plain, but the products do reach the shops. It is an imperfect answer to chronic shortages, yet better than none at all.
COLDWAR_SOV_avtovaz_the_zhiguli: On 19 April 1970 the first VAZ-2101 rolls off the assembly line in Togliatti, built under licence from Fiat on the banks of the Volga. The Zhiguli, sold abroad as the Lada, is meant to bring the private car within reach of ordinary Soviet families. Completing the giant Volga Automobile Plant would turn the dream of a car of one's own into reality for millions.
COLDWAR_SOV_kamaz_the_kama_truck_works: In Naberezhnye Chelny on the Kama River, a vast new truck plant is rising, equipped with machine tools bought from the United States, West Germany, France and Italy. Once completed, the KamAZ works will produce heavy lorries for the national economy and the army alike, replacing the ageing vehicles that slow down Soviet transport. It is one of the great construction projects of the decade.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_price_question: Soviet retail prices have barely moved in years, while production costs keep rising and the state subsidises meat, bread and milk at ever greater expense. Economists warn that artificial prices feed shortages and the black market. Yet the memory of the bloody strikes in Novocherkassk after the price rises of 1962 still haunts the leadership. Should the state dare to touch prices again?
COLDWAR_SOV_raise_retail_prices: Honest prices would close the gap between what goods cost to produce and what citizens pay for them, draining the black market of its lifeblood and filling the state budget. The reform will be deeply unpopular: queues may turn into protests, and the trade unions will bristle. But without it, the Soviet economy cannot hope to balance supply and demand.
COLDWAR_SOV_hold_the_prices: Stable prices are part of the unwritten social contract between the Party and the people. A loaf of bread is to cost the same in 1980 as it did in 1955, whatever the burden on the state budget. Shelves may be empty and queues long, but no Soviet citizen will see the price of essentials rise under this leadership.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_unified_system_question: Soviet computing stands at a crossroads. One option is to copy IBM's System/360, gaining instant access to Western software and a common standard for the entire Eastern Bloc. The other is to keep developing indigenous architectures such as Sergei Lebedev's BESM series, slower to mature but independent of Western designs. The decision will shape Soviet computing for decades.
COLDWAR_SOV_ryad_copy_the_ibm_360: The leadership decides to build the Unified System of Electronic Computers, known as Ryad, as a functional copy of the IBM System/360. Together with Comecon partners in East Germany, Hungary, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Bulgaria, Soviet factories can quickly produce compatible machines and run Western software. The price is the gradual withering of the original Soviet design schools.
COLDWAR_SOV_continue_the_besm_line: Sergei Lebedev's Institute of Precision Mechanics and Computer Engineering has created the BESM line, among the most capable computers outside the United States. Instead of copying IBM, the Soviet Union continues to invest in its own architecture, its own software and its own engineers. Progress will be slower and more expensive, but Soviet computing will remain independent and original.
COLDWAR_SOV_microelectronics_of_zelenogr: Zelenograd, a new town on the outskirts of Moscow, is the centre of Soviet microelectronics, home to research institutes and plants such as Mikron and Angstrem. Investing in its laboratories and production lines could narrow the gap with the integrated circuits of Silicon Valley. Without modern chips, neither computers nor missiles can keep pace with the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_tenth_five_year_plan: The Tenth Five-Year Plan, covering 1976 to 1980, is proclaimed the Plan of Efficiency and Quality. Instead of new factories and ever greater volumes, the emphasis shifts to productivity, technical progress and better products. The XXV Party Congress sets new priorities for the planners, but whether the ministries can change their habits remains to be seen.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_shchekino_method: At the Shchekino chemical combine near Tula, an experiment begun in 1967 allows management to reduce its workforce while keeping the wage fund unchanged, distributing the savings as higher pay to the remaining workers. Productivity soars. Extending the method across Soviet industry could free hundreds of thousands of workers for new plants, but the trade unions fear the end of guaranteed employment.
COLDWAR_SOV_quality_mark_of_the_ussr: The State Quality Mark, a pentagon bearing a stylised letter K, is awarded to Soviet products that meet the highest standards. Factories compete for the right to stamp it on their goods, and those that earn it gain bonuses and prestige. A strict certification system could improve the reputation of Soviet goods at home and in the markets of the socialist community.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_1979_economic_mechanism: In July 1979 the Central Committee and the Council of Ministers adopt a decree on improving planning and the economic mechanism. Net output replaces gross output as the key indicator, stable long-term norms are introduced and enterprises are judged on fulfilling their delivery contracts. It is the last major attempt of the Brezhnev era to make the planned economy more efficient.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_scientific_technical_rev: For years the Party has proclaimed that the scientific-technical revolution will carry socialism past capitalism. Now the promise must be fulfilled: computers, automation, new materials and modern management are to transform every branch of the economy. If science truly becomes a direct productive force, the Soviet Union can enter the twenty-first century as the most advanced society on earth.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_agrarian_problem: Agriculture is the Achilles heel of the Soviet economy. A quarter of all investment flows into the countryside, yet harvests swing wildly from year to year, collective farms remain inefficient and city dwellers still queue for meat. From the black earth of Ukraine to the virgin lands of Kazakhstan, the leadership searches for a lasting solution.
COLDWAR_SOV_pour_capital_into_the_kolkho: The orthodox answer to the agrarian crisis is more money: higher procurement prices, debt write-offs, and new barns, roads and housing for the collective and state farms. Under Brezhnev, investment in agriculture reaches unprecedented levels. The farmers welcome the funds, even if critics ask whether capital alone can cure a system that rewards plan figures rather than good harvests.
COLDWAR_SOV_fertiliser_and_machinery: Soviet fields need more fertiliser, more tractors and more combine harvesters. New chemical plants produce mineral fertilisers in vast quantities, while the tractor works of Volgograd, Kharkov and Minsk deliver modern machines to the countryside. Mechanisation and chemistry, the planners believe, will finally raise Soviet yields to the level of the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_land_melioration: The great land melioration programme, adopted in 1966, aims to transform Soviet agriculture through drainage and irrigation. Swamps in Belorussia and the Baltic are drained, while canals bring water to the dry steppes of the south. The works are costly and often poorly executed, but they promise to add millions of hectares of reliable farmland.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_non_black_earth_programm: The leadership launches a programme to revive the Non-Black-Earth zone, the historic Russian heartland stretching from Pskov to the Urals. For decades its villages have emptied while investment has gone to Ukraine and Kazakhstan. Now roads, houses, drainage and machinery are to bring the old Russian countryside back to life, even if the other republics resent the shift in priorities.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_link_system: In the 1960s the agronomist Ivan Khudenko runs an experiment in Kazakhstan with small autonomous teams, the links, which work their land independently and are paid according to results. Output soars and costs fall, yet the experiment is shut down and Khudenko is destined to die in prison. What if the leadership embraces his ideas instead and gives Soviet farmers responsibility for their own harvests?
COLDWAR_SOV_enlarge_the_private_plots: The private household plots of collective farmers cover only a tiny share of Soviet farmland, yet they produce around a quarter of the nation's food: potatoes, vegetables, eggs, milk and meat. Enlarging the plots and easing the restrictions on private livestock would quickly improve supply at little cost to the state. Orthodox ideologists grumble, but hungry cities care little for doctrine.
COLDWAR_SOV_kolkhoz_markets: In every Soviet city, the kolkhoz markets offer what the state shops cannot: fresh produce at prices set by supply and demand. Lifting the remaining restrictions on these markets would allow farmers to sell their surplus freely, improving supply and drawing trade out of the shadows. It is a small step towards the market, but a visible one.
COLDWAR_SOV_contract_farming: Instead of rigid plan targets dictated from above, collective farms and their teams sign contracts with the state to deliver fixed quantities at agreed prices. Whatever they produce beyond the contract, they may sell or keep. The system rewards initiative and efficiency, but it also loosens the grip of the district Party committees on the countryside.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_harvest_of_1972: The summer of 1972 brings disaster. After a winter of bitter frosts, drought scorches the fields of the Volga region and Ukraine, and the grain harvest falls far short of the plan. The cities face shortages of bread and the farms a lack of fodder for their livestock. The leadership must decide whether to spend precious hard currency on imports or to ask the people to endure.
COLDWAR_SOV_buy_grain_abroad: Soviet trading agencies quietly buy around a quarter of the American wheat crop at subsidised prices before Washington realises what is happening. The deal, soon dubbed the Great Grain Robbery, keeps Soviet bakeries supplied and livestock fed. From now on, the Soviet Union turns to the world market whenever its harvest fails, paying with oil and gold.
COLDWAR_SOV_tighten_the_belts: Hard currency is too precious to waste on foreign grain. Those who have lived through the war know real hardship, and they can bear this too. Livestock herds are slaughtered, rationing quietly returns to the provinces and the queues grow longer. The state preserves its reserves and its pride, but the patience of the population is not unlimited.
COLDWAR_SOV_virgin_lands_renewal: Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign has ploughed up millions of hectares of steppe in Kazakhstan and Siberia. Erosion and dust storms have since taken their toll, and yields remain unpredictable. A renewed effort with shelterbelts, crop rotation and modern machinery could restore the virgin lands as a reliable granary of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_white_gold: Cotton is the white gold of Soviet Central Asia. The Uzbek SSR alone grows most of the Union's crop, and its leader Sharof Rashidov promises ever higher harvests to Moscow. But cotton monoculture consumes vast amounts of water and labour, and behind the record figures lie inflated reports and corruption. How far should the Union push its cotton fields?
COLDWAR_SOV_irrigate_the_desert: The waters of the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya are diverted into a vast network of canals, among them the Karakum Canal, to turn the deserts of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan into cotton fields. The harvests grow and Central Asia prospers, but the rivers no longer reach the Aral Sea. Its shores begin to recede, and future generations will pay the price.
COLDWAR_SOV_save_the_aral_sea: The Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake on earth, is shrinking year by year as its rivers are drained for irrigation. Fishing towns such as Muynak and Aralsk watch the water retreat from their harbours, while salt storms spread over the fields. Reducing water consumption and modernising irrigation could save the sea, even at the expense of the cotton harvest and the patience of Tashkent.
COLDWAR_SOV_turn_the_siberian_rivers: Soviet engineers dream of reversing the flow of the great Siberian rivers. Under the project known as Sibaral, part of the waters of the Ob and the Irtysh would be channelled southwards through a canal more than two thousand kilometres long to the thirsty fields of Central Asia. It would be the most ambitious water project in history, and scientists warn of unforeseen consequences for climate and nature.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_food_programme: The Central Committee adopts the Food Programme of the USSR, a comprehensive plan to secure the nation's food supply by the end of the decade. Agriculture, processing, storage, transport and trade are to be integrated into agro-industrial complexes under unified management. After decades of half-measures, the leadership promises to solve the agrarian problem once and for all.
COLDWAR_SOV_samotlor: Discovered in 1965 among the swamps of the Tyumen region, Samotlor is the largest oil field in the Soviet Union and one of the largest in the world. Drilling crews, pipelines and new towns spring up in the West Siberian taiga, and production climbs year after year. Siberian oil is set to become the lifeblood of the economy and its most valuable export.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_tyumen_complex: West Siberia holds not only oil but also enormous deposits of natural gas. Developing them requires roads, railways, power lines and entire cities in a land of permafrost, bogs and winters far below freezing. The Tyumen oil and gas complex becomes one of the largest construction sites on earth, drawing workers from every corner of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_gas_for_pipes: Soyuznefteexport negotiates with Ruhrgas and Mannesmann over an unprecedented deal: West German large-diameter pipes on credit, repaid with deliveries of Soviet natural gas from 1973. Such an agreement would bind the Federal Republic to Soviet energy and open a lasting channel of trade across the Iron Curtain. Moscow makes its offer, and the decision now lies with Bonn.
COLDWAR_SOV_urengoy: Discovered in 1966 beyond the Arctic Circle, Urengoy is the largest gas field in the world. Bringing it into production demands drilling rigs, compressor stations and thousands of kilometres of pipeline across the tundra. Once tapped, Urengoy gas can heat Soviet cities, power industry and flow westwards to European customers who pay in hard currency.
COLDWAR_SOV_petrodollars: The oil crisis of 1973 quadruples world prices, and every barrel of Soviet oil sold abroad now brings in a fortune in hard currency. Petrodollars pay for American grain, Western machinery and generous aid to friendly regimes across the Third World. The windfall makes reform seem less urgent, and the economy grows ever more dependent on the price of oil.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_atomic_power_programme: Since the Obninsk plant began supplying the grid in 1954, the Soviet Union has seen itself as a pioneer of peaceful atomic energy. The Ministry of Medium Machine-Building and the Ministry of Energy now draw up plans for dozens of new reactors in the European part of the Union, where fossil fuels are scarce. The key question is which reactor design to build.
COLDWAR_SOV_rbmk_reactors: The RBMK is a large graphite-moderated channel reactor, derived from the military plutonium reactors. It is cheap, can be built with existing industrial capacity and can be scaled up to enormous outputs. It lacks a full containment structure and hides dangerous design flaws known only to a few specialists, but the planners value speed and size above all else.
COLDWAR_SOV_vver_reactors: The VVER is a pressurised water reactor, similar in principle to Western designs and housed within a containment structure. It is more expensive and demands advanced heavy engineering, but it is safer, more reliable and suitable for export to the socialist countries. Choosing the VVER means slower expansion, but a sounder foundation for the Soviet nuclear industry.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_leningrad_station: On the shores of the Gulf of Finland at Sosnovy Bor, the Leningrad Nuclear Power Plant takes shape, with its first unit due to go online in 1973. It is to become the flagship of Soviet nuclear energy, supplying power to the second city of the Union and its industries. Its success will set the pace for the reactors that follow across the country.
COLDWAR_SOV_atoms_for_the_republics: Nuclear power should not remain a privilege of the Russian heartland. New stations in Ukraine, Armenia, Lithuania and Kazakhstan can supply electricity to the growing cities and industries of the republics and reduce their dependence on distant coal and gas. Each new plant also binds the republics more closely to the scientific might of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_great_siberian_dams: On the Yenisei and the Angara, Soviet engineers are building some of the largest hydroelectric dams in the world. The Krasnoyarsk station nears completion, while the Sayano-Shushenskaya project, under construction since 1968, promises even greater output for the aluminium smelters and industries of Siberia. Ecologists worry about flooded valleys and lost villages, but the turbines keep turning.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_baikal_amur_mainline: The Baikal-Amur Mainline is proclaimed the construction project of the century: more than four thousand kilometres of railway through taiga, mountains and permafrost, north of Lake Baikal to the Pacific. Komsomol volunteers from every republic answer the call. The line will open up the resources of the Far East and provide a second route to the Pacific, safely distant from the Chinese border.
COLDWAR_SOV_bam_open_to_traffic: After years of labour in some of the harshest conditions on earth, the Baikal-Amur Mainline opens to regular traffic. Trains now roll from Taishet to Sovetskaya Gavan, carrying timber, coal and ore from the Far East and supplies to the garrisons along the Amur. The project of the century has become reality, and the Soviet Far East no longer depends on a single railway.
COLDWAR_SOV_kuzbass_and_ekibastuz: The Kuznetsk Basin in Western Siberia and the open-pit mines of Ekibastuz in Kazakhstan hold some of the largest coal reserves in the world. Their coal fires the power stations and steelworks of the Urals and Siberia. New mines, power plants and high-voltage lines can turn these coalfields into the energy backbone of the eastern Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_unified_energy_system: The Unified Energy System links the power grids of the Soviet republics into a single network, while the Mir interconnection extends it to the Comecon partners in Eastern Europe. Electricity can flow from Siberian dams to Ukrainian factories and from Soviet power plants to Budapest and Prague. It is socialist integration in the most literal sense.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_academy_of_sciences: The Academy of Sciences of the USSR, led by its president Mstislav Keldysh, presides over hundreds of institutes and tens of thousands of researchers. Soviet scientists rank among the best in the world in mathematics, physics and space research, yet much of their work never reaches the factories. Strengthening the Academy and its links to industry could turn scientific excellence into economic strength.
COLDWAR_SOV_akademgorodok: Near Novosibirsk, among the birch forests on the shores of the Ob Sea, stands Akademgorodok, the science town of the Academy's Siberian Branch. Its institutes of mathematics, nuclear physics and computing attract the brightest young minds, drawn by a freedom of debate unusual in the Soviet Union. Expanding the town strengthens Soviet science and computing far from the bureaucracy of Moscow.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_naukograds: Arzamas-16, Obninsk, Dubna and dozens of other science cities are missing from public maps, yet they form the backbone of Soviet nuclear, rocket and weapons research. Their residents enjoy better supplies and housing in exchange for secrecy and loyalty. Expanding the naukograds strengthens both science and defence, behind the fences and checkpoints of the KGB.
COLDWAR_SOV_genetics_rehabilitated: For decades, Trofim Lysenko's pseudo-science has dominated Soviet biology, while genuine geneticists have been dismissed, imprisoned or worse. Since his fall in 1965, the discipline has slowly been recovering. A decisive rehabilitation of genetics, with new institutes and modern breeding programmes, could bring Soviet agriculture and medicine back to the frontier of world science.
COLDWAR_SOV_scientific_exchange: Soviet and American scientists agree to found the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Laxenburg near Vienna, a meeting place for researchers from East and West. Joint commissions on space, medicine, the environment and energy follow. Opening Soviet laboratories to Western contacts accelerates research, but ideologists fear that foreign ideas will cross the border along with the data.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_space_race_question: The Americans have planted their flag on the Moon, and the Soviet lunar programme is in crisis after repeated failures of the giant N1 rocket. Should the Union continue the costly race to land a cosmonaut on the Moon, or shift its efforts to long-duration orbital stations and robotic exploration? The decision will define Soviet spaceflight for the next two decades.
COLDWAR_SOV_lunokhod: On 17 November 1970 Lunokhod 1, delivered by the Luna 17 probe, rolls onto the surface of the Sea of Rains. Steered from a control centre in Crimea, it becomes the first remote-controlled vehicle to explore another world. Robotic explorers allow the Soviet Union to claim triumphs on the Moon without risking the lives of its cosmonauts.
COLDWAR_SOV_venera: On 15 December 1970 the Venera 7 probe descends through the crushing atmosphere of Venus and transmits data from its surface, the first successful landing on another planet. Further Venera missions are to send back the first images from the Venusian surface. The exploration of the planets offers the Soviet Union a field in which it can lead the world.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_n1_moon_rocket: Sergei Korolev's giant N1 rocket is meant to carry Soviet cosmonauts to the Moon, but every launch so far has ended in an explosion, and the programme faces cancellation. What if the leadership refuses to give up? With Nikolai Kuznetsov's improved engines and patient ground testing, the N1 could yet fly and restore the prestige of the Soviet space programme.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_soviet_moonshot: The N1 finally works. A lunar orbiter and the LK lander carry a Soviet cosmonaut to the surface of the Moon, where the red flag is planted not far from the footprints of the Americans. The world press is stunned, Moscow celebrates, and the space race is suddenly far from over. Socialism has proven that it can match any achievement of the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_orbital_stations: In April 1971 Salyut 1 is set to become the first space station in history. Long-duration flights aboard orbital laboratories allow Soviet cosmonauts to conduct experiments, observe the Earth and learn to live in space for months at a time. It is a field in which the Soviet Union can lead the world, with the military Almaz stations never far behind.
COLDWAR_SOV_soyuz_apollo: An American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz are to dock in orbit, and their crews are to shake hands in space. The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project would become a powerful symbol of detente, proof that the superpowers can cooperate even in the most prestigious field of the Cold War. Moscow proposes the joint mission to Washington, and the Americans must decide whether to accept.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_space_shuttle_answer: The Americans are developing a reusable Space Shuttle, and Soviet military analysts fear it could be used to deploy weapons in orbit or even to snatch Soviet satellites. Ignoring it is not an option for a superpower. The leadership must decide how to answer, and whether to match the American programme in capability and prestige at enormous cost.
COLDWAR_SOV_energia_buran: NPO Energia, under Valentin Glushko, designs a super-heavy launch vehicle and a reusable orbiter of its own. The Energia rocket can lift a hundred tonnes into orbit, while the Buran spaceplane is designed to fly fully automatically. The programme is the most expensive in Soviet space history, but it gives the Union a capability to rival anything the Americans possess.
COLDWAR_SOV_mir_station: The era of short-lived Salyut stations gives way to a modular, permanently crewed outpost in orbit. Mir, a name meaning both peace and world, is assembled module by module and will host cosmonauts and international guests for years on end. A permanent presence in space crowns the Soviet orbital programme and demonstrates the scientific maturity of socialism.
COLDWAR_SOV_eyes_in_orbit: Since 1962, Zenit reconnaissance satellites based on the Vostok spacecraft have photographed the territory of the United States, NATO and China, returning their film capsules to Earth. Better cameras, longer missions and new generations of satellites give the General Staff an ever clearer picture of enemy forces. In the nuclear age, knowledge from orbit is a strategic weapon in itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_scientific_superpower: From the laboratories of Akademgorodok to the launch pads of Baikonur, Soviet science has become a pillar of national power. The Union trains more engineers and scientists than any other nation and competes with the United States in every field from physics to spaceflight. Science is no longer merely a tool of the state but the proud face of socialism before the world.
COLDWAR_SOV_the_soviet_army: The Soviet Army is the most powerful land force in the world: well over a hundred divisions, tens of thousands of tanks and a doctrine shaped by the experience of the Great Patriotic War. Its groups of forces stand guard in East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary, while new divisions reinforce the border with China. Maintaining its readiness is the first duty of the state.
COLDWAR_SOV_grechkos_ministry: Marshal Andrei Grechko, Minister of Defence since 1967, is a veteran of the battle for the Caucasus and a firm believer in massive conventional forces. Under his leadership the armed forces receive new tanks, missiles and infantry weapons, and the military gains a stronger voice in the Politburo. Grechko's ministry is a guarantee of strength, and a constant demand on the resources of the Union.
